knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,

library(medley)

```{r setup, echo=FALSE}
data('pisa', package = 'medley')
pisa$Private <- !pisa$Public
pisa$Public <- NULL
formula <- Private ~ .
tab <- pisa$Private |> table()
ratios <- seq(1, unname(floor(tab['FALSE'] / tab['TRUE'])))
data_public <- pisa |> dplyr::filter(!Private)
data_private <- pisa |> dplyr::filter(Private)
```

## Introduction

Statistical modeling when there is substantial imbalance in the dependent variable poses unique challenges. In these situations models often favor the majority class. Two common approaches are upsampling and downsampling. Upsampling is the process of increasing the sampling of the minority group to more closely match the size of the majority group. Conversely, downsampling involves sampling from the majority group to more closely match the size of the minority group. The latter is generally not preferred since it artificially increases the sample size (i.e. *n*) resulting in decreasing the standard error estimates.^[The $\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{n}{x}=0$ for all fixed $n$.] This paper introduces an approach where multiple logistic regression models are estimated using the minority group and a unique subset of the majority group such that all observations are majority observations are used in exactly one model while the minority group is reused across models. The final model pools the models using Rubin's Rules defined within the context of multiple imputation (Rubin, 2004).

## Impact on Fitted Values

In the United States there are broadly two types of schools, public and private. Public schools are funded by property taxes whereas privates schools charge tuition to the families. The [Programme for International Student Assessment](https://www.oecd.org/en/about/programmes/pisa.html) (PISA) is an international evaluation managed by the OECD. It measures how well 15-year-old students apply their knowledge and problem-solving skills in reading, mathematics, and science to real-world challenges. PISA samples students from both public and private schools within the United States. The `medley` package contains a subset of the PISA data for the United States containing `r nrow(pisa)` observations of `r ncol(pisa)` variables. There are `r nrow(data_public)` public school students and `r nrow(data_private)` private school students (`r unname(tab['TRUE'] / nrow(pisa)) * 100`%)

To exemplify the problem with estimating logistic regression with imbalanced data, let's consider several models where the ratio of public-to-private schools varies from 1-to-1 to 14-to-1. Figure \@ref(fig:shrinking-values) represents the distributions of the fitted values from a logistic regression with varying ratios of public-to-private schools. That is, all private school students were used in every model. For the 1-to-1 model, the first `r nrow(data_private)` public school observations, then for the 2-to-1 model the first `r 2 * nrow(data(private))` observations, etcetera until the final model uses all observations. The vertical lines correspond to the median fitted values. With all else equal, as the ratio of public-to-private schools increases, the range of fitted values shrinks towards the majority group.^[See https://psa.bryer.org/appendix-psranges.html for a simulation showing the same result.]

```{r, echo=FALSE}
fitted_values <- data.frame()
for(i in ratios) {
	df <- rbind(
		data_private,
		data_public[seq(1, i * nrow(data_private)),]
	)
	lr_out <- glm(formula, data = df, family = binomial(link = 'logit'))
	fitted_values <- rbind(fitted_values, data.frame(
		Iter = i,
		Ratio = paste0(i, ' to 1'), 
		Group = c(rep('Private', nrow(data_private)), rep('Public', i * nrow(data_private))),
		Fitted = fitted(lr_out)
	))
}
fitted_values$Ratio <- factor(fitted_values$Ratio, 
							  levels = paste0(ratios, ' to 1'),
							  ordered = TRUE)
# Keeping only odd ratios in order to make the graph less cluttered
fitted_values <- fitted_values |> dplyr::filter(Iter %% 2 == 1)

fitted_summaries <- fitted_values |>
	dplyr::group_by(Ratio, Group) |>
	dplyr::summarise(mean = mean(Fitted), 
					 median = median(Fitted),
					 .groups = "drop_last")
```

```{r shrinking-values, echo=FALSE, fig.cap='Distributions for varying public-to-private ratios. Vertical lines corrospond to the median of the fitted values.'}
ggplot(fitted_values, aes(x = Fitted, color = Group, fill = Group)) +
	geom_density(alpha = 0.2) +
	geom_vline(data = fitted_summaries, aes(xintercept = median, color = Group)) +
	facet_wrap(~ Ratio, ncol = 1, scales = 'free_y') +
	theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank()) +
	xlab('Fitted Values') + ylab('Density') +
	xlim(c(0, 1))
	# ggtitle('Distributions for varying public-to-private ratios')
```


## Stratified Modeling

The goal of stratified modeling is to address imbalance in the outcome variable while still leveraging all data. The first step is to separate the majority and minority classes. Observations in the minority class will be used in all model estimations. Observations in the majority class will be randomly assigned a model. The number of models is determined by the extent of the imbalance the specified ratio of majority-to-minority observations (the default is 1). For the PISA data here, there are approximately `r max(ratios)` times as many public school observations to private school observations. Using a ratio of one we will estimate 14 models. It should be noted that the public schools students will be used in exactly one model whereas the private school students will be used in all models. The `stratified_glm()` performs the modeling. To maximize flexibility this function can pass any parameter to the `stats::glm()` function. However, parameters that reference specific observations (e.g. `weights`, `subset`) should not be used since `stats::glm()` will be called with subsets of the data that will not match the order of the data. Similarly, the `family` parameter defaults to `binomial(link='logit')` since this method only works with classification problems with two classes.

```{r}
results <- medley::stratified_glm(
	formula = Private ~ .,
	data = pisa,
	ratio = 1
)
```

The results of all the models are combined using the `mitools::MIcombine` function (Lumley, 2026). Although this approach is designed for combining multiple imputed data sets, in this case it allows us to have a single coefficient and standard error that is not artificially smaller given a larger sample size for a model. The fitted values from all the individual models is available in the `fitted` element of the returned object. Additionally, the individual model results are available in the `model` element. The `summary()` function returns a data frame with the combined coefficients, standard error, and p-value. Below only coefficients where p < 0.1 is printed to save space.

```{r}
pisa_summary <- summary(results)
pisa_summary |> dplyr::filter(p < 0.1)
```

Figure \@ref(fig:fitted-distributions) plots the density distributions from the full model (single model using all data) and the stratified models. The stratified sample shows a distribution that spans the entire range of fitted values resulting in fitted values that are more interpretable.

```{r fitted-distributions, fig.cap='Distribution of fitted values for full and stratified models'}
plot(results)
```

Predictions for new data can be estimated using the `predict()` function.

```{r}
pisa_predicted <- predict(results, newdata = pisa)
head(pisa_predicted)
```

Figure \@ref(fig:fitted-distributions-3) shows how the stratified modeling is less effective when the ratio of public-to-private students increases to 3-to-1.

```{r fitted-distributions-3, fig.cap='Distribution of fitted values when a ratio of three is used for the stratified model'}
medley::stratified_glm(
	formula = Private ~ .,
	data = pisa,
	ratio = 3
) |> plot()
```

## Impact for Predictive Modeling

Stratified modeling clearly provides a strategy for addressing the issue of shrinking fitted values from logistic regression as imbalance in the outcome increases. In this section we will explore what impact, if any, does this approach have when modeling for prediction. To begin, we will split our data into a training and validation data set with 80% for training and 20% for validation.

```{r}
set.seed(2112); split <- medley::stratified_split(pisa, 'Private', 0.8)
pisa_train <- split$train
pisa_valid <- split$validation
pisa_train$Private |> table() |> prop.table()
pisa_valid$Private |> table() |> prop.table()
```

### Full Model

First, we will estimate the logistic regression model using the full data set.

```{r}
full_model <- glm(Private ~ ., data = pisa_train, family = binomial(link = 'logit'))
```

Get the predictions for the validation data set.

```{r}
full_new_predictions <- predict(full_model, newdata = pisa_valid, type = 'response')
```

We calculate the metrics for a receiver operating characteristic below. The summary function provides us with some thresholds that maximize accuracy, minimize cost^[Since the costs of false-positives and false-negatives are the same this will be the same threshold as maximizing accuracy], or where the specificity and sensitivity curves intersect. 

```{r}
full_roc <- medley::calculate_roc(
	predictions = full_new_predictions,
	observed = pisa_valid$Private
)
summary(full_roc)
```

Figure \@ref(fig:full-roc) represents the receiver operating characteristic plot for the validation data using the full model.

```{r full-roc, fig.cap='Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) and accuracy curves for the full model', fig.height=5, fig.width=10}
plot(full_roc)
```

In order to balance sensitivity and specificity we provide a confusion matrix using the intersection of these two curves as the cut point for determing the outcome class.

```{r}
medley::confusion_matrix(
	observed = pisa_valid$Private,
	predicted = full_new_predictions > attr(full_roc, 'intersection')
)
```

### Stratified Model

Now let's estimate the stratified model.

```{r}
stratified_model <- medley::stratified_glm(
	formula = Private ~ .,
	data = pisa_train,
	ratio = 1
)
stratified_new_predictions <- predict(stratified_model, newdata = pisa_valid)
```

Examine the receiver operating characteristics to determine the optimal cut point. Figure \@ref(fig:stratified-roc) plots the results.

```{r}
stratified_roc <- medley::calculate_roc(
	predictions = stratified_new_predictions,
	observed = pisa_valid$Private
)
summary(stratified_roc)
```

```{r stratified-roc, fig.cap='Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) and accuracy curves for the stratified model', fig.height=5, fig.width=10}
plot(stratified_roc)
```

Finally, calculate the confusion matrix using the intersection of the sensitivity and specificity curves as the cut point for determing predicted class.

```{r}
medley::confusion_matrix(
	observed = pisa_valid$Private,
	predicted = full_new_predictions > attr(stratified_roc, 'intersection')
)
```

Often introductory texts for predictive modeling and logistic regression suggest using a cut point of 0.5 for determining the class. As show above, this is not the optimal cut point when there is significant imbalance. The stratified modeling approach introduced gets us closer to that intuitive cut point in the middle. It should be noted that this approach is no better or worse for making predictions. However, it does address the issue of shrinking fitted values and makes the fitted and predicted values more interpretable.


## Conclusion

The stratified modeling approach provides a modeling approach for logistic regression where interpretability of the fitted or predicted values are meaningful. For predictive modeling adjusting the cut point for making a class prediction will provide a similar result. However, this issue was initially encountered when conducting propensity score analysis (PSA). Logistic regression is often used to estimate the propensity scores, which are defined as the conditional probability of being in the treatment (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983). When using logistic regression, the propensity scores are simply the fitted values from the model. In this context having fitted values that span the entire range where the distribution of the treatment group (private schools in this example) is skewed to the right and the control group (public schools in this example) is skewed to the left. For these situations the stratified modeling approach may provide a reasonable approach to addressing the issue of shrinking fitted values from logistic regression with significant imbalance.
